# Unit Speed Curves
## Definition 1
Let $\alpha: (a, b) \to \mathbb{R}^3$ be a regular unit speed curve.

**(i)** The ***tangent vector field*** is the map $T(s) = \alpha'(s)$.

**(ii)** The ***curvature*** of $\alpha$ is the map $\kappa(s) = \| T'(s) \|$.

**(iii)** The ***normal vector field*** is the map $N(s) = \frac{T'(s)}{\kappa(s)}$.

**(iv)** The ***binormal vector field*** is the map $B(s) = T(s) \times N(s)$.

**(v)** The ***torsion*** of $\alpha$ is the map $\tau(s) = - \langle B'(s), N(s) \rangle$.

**(vi)** The ***Frenet-Serret appratus*** of $\alpha$ is the set $\{ T(s), N(s), B(s), \kappa(s), \tau(s) \}$.

곡선 $\alpha$는 단위 스피드 곡선으로 들고 왔음을 유의하자. 단위 스피드가 아니라면 위와 같은 공식으로 계산할 수 없다. 또한 곡률은 항상 $0$ 이상의 값을 갖는데, 만약 곡률이 $0$이라면 그 곡선은 사실상 직선이 되고, $N, B, \tau$가 모두 정의되지 않음을 기억하자.

$T$는 말 그대로 각 점에서의 곡선에 접하는 접선 벡터다. 한편 곡률 $\kappa$는 $T$의 도함수의 크기로 정의되는데, 곡선이 **많이 굽어있을수록** $T$는 급격하게 변하고, 다시 말해 $T'$의 크기는 커진다. 반면 곡선이 **많이 굽어있지 않고 평평할수록** $T$는 별로 변하지 않고, 다시 말해 $T'$의 크기는 작아진다. 이렇듯 곡률, 즉 곡선이 굽어있는 정도는 접선벡터의 변화량의 크기로 정의하는 것이 직관적이라는 사실을 알 수 있다.

다음과 같이 $xy$ 평면에 속하는 곡선 $\alpha(s) = (x(s), y(s)), \forall s \in (a,b)$을 고려하자. 만약 $\alpha$가 단위 속력 곡선이라면 $\{ x'(s) \}^2 + \{ y'(s) \}^2 = 1$이 성립하고, 따라서 $\alpha(s) = (\cos(\theta(s)), \sin(\theta(s)))$과 같이 표현할 수 있게 된다. 이때 곡률을 계산해보면

$$\begin{align*}
\kappa(s) &= \| T'(s) \| \\
&= \| (-\sin(\theta(s)) \cdot \theta'(s), \cos(\theta(s)) \cdot \theta'(s)) \| \\
&= \vert \theta'(s) \|
\end{align*}$$

을 얻는다. 즉 위와 같이 곡률을 정의하는 방법이 직관적임과 더불어 합리적이라는 사실을 알 수 있다.

한편 $T$은 곡선에 접하는 방향을 가지는 벡터인 반면 $T'$은 $T$에 수직한 방향을 갖는다. 이해를 위해 평면 상에서 위로 볼록한 이차함수와 같은 꼴로 곡선이 놓여 있다고 생각해보자. 이때 접선 벡터 $T$가 변하는 방향을 생각하면 곡선의 "안쪽"으로 변하는 사실을 알 수 있다. 다시 말해 $T$가 변하는 방향은 늘 곡선의 "안쪽"을 가리키는 것이고, 때문에 $T'$은 $T$와 수직하되 곡선의 안쪽을 향하는 방향을 가진다. 이때 노말 벡터 $N$은 $T'$의 방향을 가지는 단위 벡터로 정의된다.

좀 더 물리적인 센스로 생각해본다면, $N$은 일종의 "외력"의 방향을 가리킨다고 볼 수 있다. 곡선을 어떤 입자가 공간 상에서 이동해나가는 궤적, 혹은 경로라고 볼 때, 만약 입자가 어떠한 외력도 받지 않는다면 현재의 관성을 유지한 채 운동 상태를 유지할 것이고, 어떤 초기속도를 가지고 있었다면 그 초기속도를 따라 직선 궤도를 그리며 나아갈 것이다. 이는 다시 말해 전혀 굽어있지 않은 상태를 의미한다. 반면 입자가 어떤 외력을 받고 있다면 궤도가 외력이 가하는 방향으로 휘게 될 것이고, 이는 $T'$이 곡선의 안쪽 방향을 가진다는 사실과 일맥상통한다.

그리고 $T$와 $N$의 외적으로 만들어지는 바이노말 벡터 $B$는 $T$와 $N$이 만드는 평면에 수직한 벡터인데, 물리적으로는 어떤 순간에 입자가 회전하는 회전축 방향을 가리킨다고 이해할 수 있다. 마지막으로 토션은 $B$의 $N$방향의 변화율이라고 볼 수 있는데, 직관적으로는 **곡선이 꼬여있는 정도**를 의미한다고 받아들일 수 있다. $\mathbb{R}^3$에서 $z$축을 향하여 일정하게 올라가는 나선(helix)을 생각해보자. $N$은 항상 $z$축을 향할 것이고, $B$는 시간이 지날수록 이리저리 흔들리며 뱅글뱅글 도는 방향으로 변하게 될 것이다. 직관적으로 $B'$의 $N$방향 성분을 측정하면 외력이 작용함에 따라 회전축이 얼마나 흔들리는지 측량할 수 있다. 곡선이 더 극단적으로 꼬여있을수록 그 변화율은 더욱 커질 것이고, 곡선이 흔들리지 않고 안정적으로 놓여있을수록 그 변화율은 더욱 적어진다. 만약 곡선이 한 평면 안에 완전히 속해 있다면, 다시 말해 입자가 일정한 회전축을 가진 채 운동한다면 곡선은 전혀 꼬여있지 않다고 이해할 수 있고, 실제로도 토션은 항상 $0$의 값을 갖는다.

한편, 이렇게 정의한 세 개의 벡터 $T(s), N(s), B(s)$는 각각 단위벡터이면서 서로 직교한다. 또한 전체 공간이 $\mathbb{R}^3$이므로 집합 $\{ T(s), N(s), B(s) \}$는 $\mathbb{R}^3$의 기저를 이룬다. 다시 말해 곡선 위의 점 $s$이 주어질 때마다 그 점에 의존하는 $\mathbb{R}^3$의 정규직교기저가 주어지는 것이다. 

### Example
**(i)** Consider the curve $\alpha(s) = \left(r \cos \frac{s}{r}, r \sin \frac{s}{r}, 0 \right), \forall s \in (a,b)$. Then $\alpha$ is a unit speed curve, and we have

$$\begin{align*}
\kappa(s) &= \| T'(s) \| \\
&= \left\| \left( -\frac{1}{r} \sin \frac{s}{r}, \frac{1}{r} \cos \frac{s}{r}, 0 \right) \right\| \\
&= \sqrt{\left( -\frac{1}{r} \sin \frac{s}{r} \right)^2 + \left( \frac{1}{r} \cos \frac{s}{r} \right)^2} \\
&= \sqrt{\frac{1}{r^2} \left( \sin^2 \frac{s}{r} + \cos^2 \frac{s}{r} \right)} \\
&= \frac{1}{r}. \end{align*}$$

Furthermore, note that

$$\begin{align*}
N(s) &= \left( -\cos \frac{s}{r}, -\sin \frac{s}{r}, 0 \right), \\
B(s) &= T(s) \times N(s) \\
&= \begin{vmatrix} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ -\sin \frac{s}{r} & \cos \frac{s}{r} & 0 \\ -\cos \frac{s}{r} & -\sin \frac{s}{r} & 0 \end{vmatrix} \\
&= \mathbf{k} = (0, 0, 1). 
\end{align*}$$

Thus, we have

$$\begin{align*}
\tau(s) &= - \langle B'(s), N(s) \rangle \\
&= 0.
\end{align*}$$

즉 원의 경우 곡률은 모든 점에 대해서 반지름의 역수인 $\frac{1}{r}$로 일정하고, 한 평면에 완전히 속해 있으므로 토션은 $0$임을 알 수 있다.

## Theorem 1
Let $\alpha(s)$ be a unit speed curve.

**(i)** For each $s$ such that $\kappa(s) \neq 0$, the set $\{ T(s), N(s), B(s) \}$ is an orthonormal basis of $\mathbb{R}^3$, called the ***Frenet-Serret frame***.

**(ii)** $\kappa \equiv 0$ $\iff$ $\alpha$ is a straight line $\iff$ $\exists x_0 \in \mathbb{R}^3$ such that every tangent line to $\alpha$ passes through $x_0$.

### Proof
**(i)** By construction, we have that $\| T(s) \| = 1 = \| N(s) \|$, $B(s) \perp T(s)$ and $B(s) \perp N(s)$. Note that

$$\begin{align*}
1 &= \| T(s) \|^2 \\
&= \langle T(s), T(s) \rangle \\
\implies 0 &= \frac{d}{ds} \langle T(s), T(s) \rangle \\
&= 2 \langle T(s), T'(s) \rangle \\
\implies 0 &= \langle T(s), N(s) \rangle,
\end{align*}$$

so $T(s) \perp N(s)$.

Note that $\| B(s) \| = \| T(s) \| \| N(s) \| = 1$ since $B(s)$ is defined as $T(s) \times N(s)$. Thus $\{ T(s), N(s), B(s) \}$ is an orthonormal basis of $\mathbb{R}^3$.

**(ii)** Since $\kappa(s) = \| T'(s) \| = 0$, we have $T'(s) = 0$, so $T(s) = c$ for some constant vector $c \in \mathbb{R}^3$. By the fundamental theorem of calculus, we have

$$\begin{align*}
\alpha(s) &= \int_a^s \alpha'(u) du + \alpha(a) \\
&= \int_a^s T(u) du + \alpha(a) \\
&= c(s-a) + \alpha(a),
\end{align*}$$

which is the equation of a straight line.

Suppose that $\alpha$ is a straight line. Note that each tangent line to $\alpha$ is the same as $\alpha$. If we choose any point $x_0$ on $\alpha$, then every tangent line to $\alpha$ passes through $x_0$.

Suppose that every tangent line to $\alpha$ passes through some point $x_0$. Then we have

$$\alpha(s) - x_0 = \lambda(s)T(s)$$

for some scalar function $\lambda(s)$. Since $\langle \alpha(s) - x_0, T(s) \rangle = \lambda(s)$ and $\alpha(s)$ and $T(s)$ are differentiable on $(a,b)$, $\lambda(s)$ is differentiable on $(a,b)$. 

If $\kappa \equiv 0$, then we are done. If we assume $\kappa \not \equiv 0$, then there is some interval such that the normal vector $N(s)$ is defined. Then 

$$\begin{align*}
T(s) &= \lambda'(s)T(s) + \lambda(s)T'(s) \\
&= \lambda'(s)T(s) + \lambda(s)\kappa(s)N(s).
\end{align*}$$

Hence $(\lambda'(s) - 1)T(s) + \lambda(s)\kappa(s)N(s) = 0$, which implies that $\lambda'(s) = 1$ and $\lambda(s)\kappa(s) = 0$. These two condition contradicts each other, so we must have that $\kappa \equiv 0$. $\blacksquare$

## Frenet-Serret Formula
Let $\alpha(s)$ be a unit speed curve with $\kappa \not \equiv 0$, and let $\{ T(s), N(s), B(s), \kappa(s), \tau(s) \}$ be a Frenet-Serret appartus of $\alpha$ at $s$. Then we have:

**(i)** $T'(s) = \kappa(s) N(s)$

**(ii)** $N'(s) = -\kappa(s) T(s) + \tau(s) B(s)$

**(iii)** $B'(s) = -\tau(s) N(s)$

In matrix form,

$$\begin{bmatrix}
T' \\
N' \\
B'
\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}
0 & \kappa & 0 \\
-\kappa & 0 & \tau \\
0 & -\tau & 0
\end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix}
T \\
N \\
B
\end{bmatrix}.$$

$B'$을 잘 보면 오직 $N$에만 의존하는 걸 알 수 있는데, 다시 말해 바이노말 벡터는 $T$나 그 자신 $B$ 방향으로 변하지 않고 오직 $N$ 방향으로만 변한다는 것이다. 또한 그 비례 상수가 토션으로 주어지는데, 토션의 정의 자체가 $B'$의 $N$ 방향 변화량으로 정의되었기 때문에 자연스럽게 이해할 수 있다. 뒤집어서 말하면, 토션이 $0$이면 $B$는 변하지 않고, 이는 주어진 커브가 어떤 한 평면에 완전히 속하게 됨을 알 수 있다.

::: {.callout-note title="Proof" collapse="true" icon=false}
Note that each vector $v$ in $\mathbb{R}^3$ can be expressed as:

$$v = \langle v, T \rangle T + \langle v, N \rangle N + \langle v, B \rangle B.$$

**(i)** By definition of the normal vector $N(s) = \frac{T'(s)}{\kappa(s)}$, we have $T'(s) = \kappa(s) N(s)$.

**(ii)** Note that 

1. $\langle N', N \rangle = 0$.

$\big[ (\because)$

$$\begin{align*}
1 &= \langle N, N \rangle \\
\implies 0 &= \frac{d}{ds} \langle N, N \rangle \\
&= \langle N', N \rangle + \langle N, N' \rangle \\
&= 2 \langle N', N \rangle \\
\implies \langle N', N \rangle &= 0.\big]
\end{align*}$$

2. $\langle N', T \rangle = - \kappa$

$\big[ (\because)$ 

$$\begin{align*}
\frac{d}{ds} \langle N, T \rangle &= \langle N', T \rangle + \langle N, T' \rangle \\
&= \langle N', T \rangle + \langle N, \kappa N \rangle \\
&= \langle N', T \rangle + \kappa \| N \|^2 \\
&= \langle N', T \rangle + \kappa \\
\implies \langle N', T \rangle &= - \kappa.\big]
\end{align*}$$

Since $N' = \langle N', T \rangle T + \langle N', N \rangle N + \langle N', B \rangle B = -\kappa T + \tau B$, we have $N' = -\kappa T + \tau B$.

**(iii)** Note that

1. $\langle B', B \rangle = 0$.

$\big[ (\because)$

$$\begin{align*}
1 &= \langle B, B \rangle \\
\implies 0 &= \frac{d}{ds} \langle B, B \rangle \\
&= \langle B', B \rangle + \langle B, B' \rangle \\
&= 2 \langle B', B \rangle \\
\implies \langle B', B \rangle &= 0.\big]
\end{align*}$$

2. $\langle B', T \rangle = 0$.

$\big[ (\because)$ 

$$\begin{align*}
\frac{d}{ds} \langle B, T \rangle &= \langle B', T \rangle + \langle B, T' \rangle \\
&= \langle B', T \rangle + \langle B, \kappa N \rangle \\
&= \langle B', T \rangle + \kappa \langle B, N \rangle \\
&= \langle B', T \rangle + \kappa \cdot 0 \\
&= \langle B', T \rangle \\
\implies \langle B', T \rangle &= 0.\big]
\end{align*}$$

Since $B' = \langle B', T \rangle T + \langle B', N \rangle N + \langle B', B \rangle B = \tau N$, we have $B' = \tau N$. $\blacksquare$
:::

## Definition 2
Let $\alpha(s)$ be a unit speed curve, and let $\{ T(s), N(s), B(s) \}$ be a Frenet-Serret frame of $\alpha$.

**(i)** The ***osculating plane*** to $\alpha$ at the point $\alpha(s)$ is the plane through $\alpha(s)$ spanned by $T(s)$ and $N(s)$ (and hence perpendicular to $B(s)$).

**(ii)** The ***normal plane*** to $\alpha$ at the point $\alpha(s)$ is the plane through $\alpha(s)$ spanned by $N(s)$ and $B(s)$ (and hence perpendicular to $T(s)$).

**(iii)** The ***rectifying plane*** to $\alpha$ at the point $\alpha(s)$ is the plane through $\alpha(s)$ spanned by $T(s)$ and $B(s)$ (and hence perpendicular to $N(s)$).

## Theorem 2
Let $\alpha(s): (a, b) \to \mathbb{R}^3$ be a unit speed curve, and let $\{ \kappa(s), \tau(s), T(s), N(s), B(s) \}$ be a Frenet-Serret apparatus of $\alpha$ where $\kappa \not \equiv 0$.

**(i)** $\tau \equiv 0$ $\iff$ $\alpha$ is a plane curve $\iff$ $B(s)$ is a constant vector.

**(ii)** $\alpha$ is a part of circle of radius $\frac{1}{\kappa}$ $\iff$ $\kappa \equiv C$ for some positive constant $C > 0$ and $\tau \equiv 0$.

**(iii)** Every normal plane to $\alpha$ passes through a fixed point $\iff$ $\alpha$ lies on a sphere.

**(iv)** Every osculating plane to $\alpha$ is parallel $\iff$ $\tau \equiv 0$.

**(v)** Suppose that $\alpha$ lies on a sphere of radius $r$ and center $m$. If $\tau \not \equiv 0$, then

$$\alpha - m = - \rho N - \rho'\sigma B$$

where $\displaystyle \rho = \frac{1}{\kappa}$ and $\sigma = \frac{1}{\tau}$.

### Proof
**(i)** Suppose that $\tau \equiv 0$. By the Frenet-Serret formula, $B' \equiv 0$, so $B$ is a constant vector. We claim that $\langle \alpha(s) - \alpha(s_0), B(s) \rangle = 0$ for any $s, s_0$.

$$\begin{align*}
\frac{d}{ds} \langle \alpha(s) - \alpha(s_0), B(s) \rangle &= \langle \alpha'(s), B(s) \rangle + \langle \alpha(s) - \alpha(s_0), B'(s) \rangle \\
&= \langle T(s), B(s) \rangle + \langle \alpha(s) - \alpha(s_0), 0 \rangle \\
&= 0,
\end{align*}$$

so we have $\langle \alpha(s) - \alpha(s_0), B(s) \rangle = c$ for some constant $c$. Taking $s = s_0$, we obtain $c = 0$. Thus, $\langle \alpha(s) - \alpha(s_0), B(s) \rangle = 0$, which means that $\alpha(s)$ lies in the plane through $\alpha(s_0)$ and perpendicular to $B(s)$. 

Suppose that $\alpha$ is a plane curve. WLOG, we can assume that $\alpha$ lies in the $xy$-plane, i.e. $\alpha(s) = (x(s), y(s), 0)$ for some scalar functions $x(s), y(s)$. Then we have

$$\begin{align*}
T(s) &= (x'(s), y'(s), 0), \\
N(s) &= \frac{T'(s)}{\kappa(s)} = \frac{(x''(s), y''(s), 0)}{\kappa(s)}, \\
B(s) &= T(s) \times N(s) = \begin{vmatrix} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ x'(s) & y'(s) & 0 \\ x''(s)/\kappa(s) & y''(s)/\kappa(s) & 0 \end{vmatrix} = \left(0, 0, \frac{x'y'' - y'x''}{\kappa(s)} \right).
\end{align*}$$

Since $\vert B(s) \vert = 1$ and $B$ is continuous, we obtain $\frac{x'y'' - y'x''}{\kappa(s)} = \pm 1$. Thus, $B$ is a constant vector.

Suppose that $B$ is a constant vector. By the Frenet-Serret formula, we have $B' = \tau N = 0$. Since $N \neq 0$, we obtain $\tau = 0$.

**(ii)** $(\implies)$ Suppose that $\alpha$ is a part of circle of radius $\frac{1}{\kappa}$. Then $\kappa$ is a positive constant and it is a plane curve, so $\tau \equiv 0$ by **(i)**. 

$(\impliedby)$ Suppose that $\kappa \equiv C > 0$ and $\tau \equiv 0$. Let $r(s) = \alpha(s) + \frac{1}{\kappa}N(s)$. Then 

$$\begin{align*}
r'(s) &= \alpha'(s) + \frac{1}{\kappa}N'(s) \\
&= T(s) + \frac{1}{\kappa}(-\kappa T(s)) \\
&= 0,
\end{align*}$$

so that $r(s) = C$ for some constant vector $C$. Then

$$\begin{align*}
\| r(s) - \alpha(s) \| &= \| \frac{1}{\kappa} N(s) \| \\
&= \frac{1}{\kappa}.
\end{align*}$$

which means that $\alpha$ is a part of circle of radius $\frac{1}{\kappa}$. 

**(iii)** $(\implies)$ Suppose that every normal plane to $\alpha$ passes through a fixed point $m$. Note that $\alpha(s) - m$ lies in a normal plane at $\alpha(s)$, which means that $\langle \alpha(s) - m, T(s) \rangle = 0$. Then 

$$\begin{align*}
\frac{d}{ds} \langle \alpha(s) - m, \alpha(s) - m \rangle &= 2 \langle \alpha(s) - m, T(s) \rangle = 0,
\end{align*}$$

so that $\| \alpha(s) - m \| = \langle \alpha(s) - m, \alpha(s) - m \rangle$ is a constant. Hence $\alpha$ lies in a sphere.

$(\impliedby)$ Suppose that $\alpha$ lies in a sphere of radius $r$ centered at $m$. Then $\| \alpha(s) - m \|^2 = r^2$. Differentiating, $\langle \alpha(s) - m, T(s) \rangle = 0$. Note that the equation of a normal plane at $\alpha(s)$ is $\langle x - \alpha(s), T(s) \rangle = 0$. Since the center $m$ always satisfies $\langle m - \alpha(s), T(s) \rangle = 0$, $m$ is on every normal plane.

**(iv)** $(\implies)$ Suppose that every osculating plane to $\alpha$ is parallel. Then $B(s)$ at any two points are parallel, which implies that $B(s)$ is a constant. Hence, $\tau \equiv 0$.

$(\impliedby)$ Suppose that $\tau \equiv 0$. Then $\alpha$ is a plane curve, which means that every osculating plane to $\alpha$ is parallel.

**(v)** Suppose that $\alpha$ lies in a sphere of radius $r$ centered at $m$ and $\tau \not \equiv 0$. Then $\| \alpha(s) - m \|^2 = r^2$. Differentiating, we have $\langle \alpha(s) - m, T(s) \rangle = 0$. Differentiating again,

$$\begin{align*}
0 &= \langle \alpha(s) - m, T'(s) \rangle + \langle T(s), T(s) \rangle \\
&= \langle \alpha(s) - m, \kappa(s)N(s) \rangle + 1,
\end{align*}$$

which implies that $\kappa(s) \neq 0$ and $\langle \alpha(s) - m, N(s) \rangle = -\frac{1}{\kappa(s)}$.

Note that

$$\begin{align*}
\alpha(s) - m &= \langle \alpha(s) - m, T(s) \rangle T(s) + \langle \alpha(s) - m, N(s) \rangle N(s) + \langle \alpha(s) - m, B(s) \rangle B(s) \\
&= - \frac{1}{\kappa(s)} N(s) + \langle \alpha(s) - m, B(s) \rangle B(s) \\
&= - \rho(s) N(s) + \langle \alpha(s) - m, B(s) \rangle B(s)
\end{align*}$$

Differentiating $\langle \alpha(s) - m, N(s) \rangle = - \rho(s)$, we have

$$\begin{align*}
-\rho'(s) &= \langle T(s), N(s) \rangle + \langle \alpha(s) - m, N'(s) \rangle \\
&= \langle \alpha(s) - m, - \kappa(s) T(s) + \tau(s) B(s) \rangle \\
&= \tau(s) \langle \alpha(s) - m, B(s) \rangle, 
\end{align*}$$

so that $\langle \alpha(s) - m, B(s) \rangle = -\frac{\rho'(s)}{\tau(s)} = - \rho'(s) \sigma(s)$.

Hence, we obtain

$$\alpha(s) - m = - \rho N - \rho' \sigma B. \blacksquare$$

# Non-unit Speed Curves

## Definition 3
Let $\beta: [a, b] \to \mathbb{R}^3$ be a regular curve, and let $t = t(s)$ be the arc length reparametrization where $s(t) = \int_a^t \| \beta'(u) \| du$. Then $\alpha(s) := \beta(t(s))$ is a unit speed curve. For the Frenet-Serret apparatus $\{\kappa(s), \tau(s), T(s), N(s), B(s)\}$ of $\alpha$, we define ***the Frenet-Serret apparatus of $\beta$*** by

$$\begin{align*}
\kappa_{\beta}(t) &= \kappa(s(t)), \\
\tau_{\beta}(t) &= \tau(s(t)), \\
T_{\beta}(t) &= T(s(t)), \\
N_{\beta}(t) &= N(s(t)), \\
B_{\beta}(t) &= B(s(t)).
\end{align*}$$

본래 프레네-세레 도구는 단위 스피드 곡선에 대해서만 정의했지만, 여기서는 단위 스피드가 아닌 정칙 곡선에 대해서도 정의한다. 정칙 곡선은 항상 길이 재매개변수화를 통해 단위 스피드 곡선으로 나타낼 수 있고, 여기서 프레네-세레 도구를 정의한 뒤 거꾸로 재매개변수화를 적용시켜서 정의해준다. 그러면 각 도구들을 계산하는 방법 또한 달라질 것이고, 구체적인 공식은 아래와 같이 주어진다.

## Theorem 3
Let $\beta$ be a regular curve, and let $\{ \kappa, \tau, T, N, B \}$ be the Frenet-Serret apparatus of $\beta$. Then 

**(i)** $T = \frac{\dot{\beta}}{\| \dot{\beta} \|}$

**(ii)** $B = \frac{\dot{\beta} \times \ddot{\beta}}{\| \dot{\beta} \times \ddot{\beta} \|}$

**(iii)** $N = T \times B$

**(iv)** $\kappa = \frac{\| \dot{\beta} \times \ddot{\beta} \|}{\| \dot{\beta} \|^3}$

**(v)** $\tau = \frac{\big[\dot{\beta}, \ddot{\beta}, \dddot{\beta}\big]}{\| \dot{\beta} \times \ddot{\beta} \|^2}$

$\dot{\beta}, \ddot{\beta}, \dddot{\beta}$는 각각 $\beta$를 $t$에 대해서 한 번 미분, 두 번 미분, 세 번 미분한 기호이다. $\alpha$는 $s$를 변수로 가지고 $\beta$는 $t$를 변수로 가지기 때문에 어떤 변수로 미분했는지 구분해줄 필요가 있다. $s$로 미분했을 경우 $\alpha'$, $t$로 미분했을 경우 $\dot{\beta}$와 같이 쓴다.

::: {.callout-note title="Proof" collapse="true" icon=false}
Let $\{ \kappa_\alpha, \tau_\alpha, T_\alpha, N_\alpha, B_\alpha \}$ and $\{ \kappa_\beta, \tau_\beta, T_\beta, N_\beta, B_\beta \}$ be the Frenet-Serret apparatus of $\alpha$ and $\beta$ respectively.

**(i)** Note that $\dot{s}(t) = \| \dot{\beta}(t) \|$. Since $\beta(t) = \alpha(s(t))$, we have 

$$\begin{align*}
dot{\beta}(t) &= \alpha'(s(t)) \dot{s}(t) \\
&= T_\alpha(s(t)) \| \dot{\beta}(t) \| \\
&= T_\beta(t) \| \dot{\beta}(t) \|.
\end{align*}$$

Hence, $T_\beta(t) = \frac{\dot{\beta}(t)}{\| \dot{\beta}(t) \|}$.

**(iv)** From **(i)** and the Frenet-Serret formula, we have

$$\begin{align*}
\ddot{\beta}(t) &= \frac{d}{dt} \left( T_\alpha(s(t)) \dot{s}(t) \right) \\
&= T'_\alpha(s(t)) \dot{s}(t)^2 + T_\alpha(s(t)) \ddot{s}(t) \\
&= \kappa_\alpha(s(t)) N_\alpha(s(t)) \dot{s}(t)^2 + T_\alpha(s(t)) \ddot{s}(t).
\end{align*}$$

Then

$$\begin{align*}
\dot{\beta}(t) \times \ddot{\beta}(t) &= (T_\alpha(s(t)) \| \dot{\beta}(t) \|) \times (\kappa_\alpha(s(t)) N_\alpha(s(t)) \dot{s}(t)^2 + T_\alpha(s(t)) \ddot{s}(t)) \\
&= \kappa_\alpha(s(t)) \dot{s}^3(t) B_\alpha(s(t)) \\
&= \kappa_\beta(t) \| \dot{\beta}(t) \|^3 B_\beta(t).
\end{align*}$$

Hence, $\kappa_\beta(t) = \frac{\| \dot{\beta}(t) \times \ddot{\beta}(t) \|}{\| \dot{\beta}(t) \|^3}$.

**(ii)** Suppose that $\| \dot{\beta} \times \ddot{\beta} \| \neq 0$. From **(iv)**, we have $\| \dot{\beta}(t) \times \ddot{\beta}(t) \| = \kappa_\beta(t) \| \dot{\beta}(t) \|^3$. Thus,

$$\begin{align*}
B_\beta(t) &= \frac{\dot{\beta}(t) \times \ddot{\beta}(t)}{\| \kappa_\beta(t) \| \| \dot{\beta}(t) \|^3} \\
&= \frac{\dot{\beta}(t) \times \ddot{\beta}(t)}{\kappa_\beta(t) \| \dot{\beta}(t) \|^3}.
\end{align*}$$

**(iii)** 

$$\begin{align*}
N_\beta(t) &= N_\alpha(s(t)) \\
&= B_\alpha(s(t)) \times T_\alpha(s(t)) \\
&= B_\beta(t) \times T_\beta(t).
\end{align*}$$

**(v)** From (iv) and the Frenet-Serret formula, we have

$$\begin{align*}
\dddot{\beta}(t) &= \frac{d}{dt}(\kappa_\alpha(s(t)) \dot{s}(t)^2 \\
&= \frac{d}{dt}(\kappa_\alpha(s(t)) \dot{s}(t)^2 N_\alpha(s(t)) + T_\alpha(s(t)) \ddot{s}(t)) \\
&= \frac{d}{dt}(\kappa_\alpha(s(t))\dot{s}(t)^2) N_\alpha(s(t)) + \kappa_\alpha(s(t))\dot{s}(t)^3 N'_\alpha(s(t)) + \dddot{s}(t) T_\alpha(s(t)) + \ddot{s}(t) T'_\alpha(s(t)) \dot{s}(t) \\
&= \frac{d}{dt}(\kappa_\alpha(s(t))\dot{s}(t)^2) N_\alpha(s(t)) + \kappa_\alpha(s(t))\dot{s}(t)^3 (-\kappa_\alpha(s(t)) T_\alpha(s(t)) + \tau_\alpha(s(t)) B_\alpha(s(t))) \\
& \quad + \dddot{s}(t) T_\alpha(s(t)) + \ddot{s}(t) (\kappa_\alpha(s(t)) N_\alpha(s(t)) \dot{s}(t)) \\
&= (\dddot{s}(T) - \kappa_\alpha^2\dot{s}^3)T_\alpha(s(t)) + (\ddot{s}(t)\dot{s}(t)\kappa_\alpha(s(t)) + \frac{d}{dt}(\kappa_\alpha(s(t)))N_\alpha(s(t)) + \kappa_\alpha\dot{s}^3\tau_\alpha(s(t)) B_\alpha(s(t)).
\end{align*}$$

Hence,

$$\begin{align*}
\big[\dot{\beta}, \ddot{\beta}, \dddot{\beta}\big] &= \langle \kappa_\beta(t) \dot{s}^3(t) B_\beta(t), \kappa_\beta(t)\dot{s}^3(t)\tau_\beta(t) B_\beta(t) \rangle \\
&= \kappa^2_\beta(t) \tau_\beta(t) \dot{s}^6(t) \\
&= (\kappa_\beta(t) \| \dot{\beta}(t) \|^3)^2 \tau_\beta(t).
\end{align*}$$

Since $\| \dot{\beta}(t) \times \ddot{\beta}(t) \| = \kappa_\beta(t) \| \dot{\beta}(t) \|^3$, we have

$$\tau_\beta(t) = \frac{\big[\dot{\beta}, \ddot{\beta}, \dddot{\beta}\big]}{\| \dot{\beta}(t) \times \ddot{\beta}(t) \|^2}. \blacksquare$$
:::

## Frenet-Serret Formula
Let $\beta$ be a regular curve, and let $\{ \kappa, \tau, T, N, B \}$ be the Frenet-Serret apparatus of $\beta$. Then

**(i)** $T'(s) = \kappa(s) \| \dot{\beta} \| N(s)$

**(ii)** $N'(s) = -\kappa(s) \| \dot{\beta} \| T(s) + \tau(s) \| \dot{\beta} \| B(s)$

**(iii)** $B'(s) = -\tau(s) \| \dot{\beta} \| N(s)$

In matrix form,

$$\begin{bmatrix}
T' \\
N' \\
B'
\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}
0 & \kappa \| \dot{\beta} \| & 0 \\
-\kappa \| \dot{\beta} \| & 0 & \tau \| \dot{\beta} \| \\
0 & -\tau \| \dot{\beta} \| & 0
\end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix}
T \\
N \\
B
\end{bmatrix}.$$

# Fundamental Theorem of Curve
Let $(a, b)$ be an open interval containing zero. Let $\overline{\kappa}(s) > 0$ be a $C^1$ function on $(a, b)$, and let $\overline{\tau}(s)$ be a continuous function on $(a, b)$. Let $x_0 \in \mathbb{R}^3$, and let $\{ D, E, F \}$ be a right handed orthonormal basis of $\mathbb{R}^3$. Then there exists a unique $C^3$ regular curve $\alpha: (a, b) \to \mathbb{R}^3$ with the arc length parameter from $\alpha(0)$ such that

$$\begin{align*}
\alpha(0) &= x_0 \\
T(0) &= D \\
N(0) &= E \\
B(0) &= F \\
\kappa(s) &= \overline{\kappa}(s) \\
\tau(s) &= \overline{\tau}(s)
\end{align*}$$

## Proof
::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Picard's Theorem
Let each of the $n$ functions $F_1, \ldots, F_n$ and the $n^2$ first partial derivatives $\frac{\partial F_1}{\partial x_1}, \ldots, \frac{\partial F_1}{\partial x_n}, \ldots, \frac{\partial F_n}{\partial x_1}, \ldots, \frac{\partial F_n}{\partial x_n}$ be continuous in a region $R$ of $t x_1 x_2 \cdots x_n$-space defined by 

$$\alpha < t < \beta, \quad \alpha_1 < x_1 < \beta_1, \quad \ldots, \quad \alpha_n < x_n < \beta_n,$$

and let the point $(t_0, x_1^0, x_2^0, \ldots, x_n^0) \in R$.

Then there is an interval $|t - t_0| < h$ in which there exists a unique solution

$$ x_1 = \phi_1(t), \quad \ldots, \quad x_n = \phi_n(t) $$

of the system of differential equations

$$x_1' = F_1(t, x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n), \\ x_2' = F_2(t, x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n), \\ \vdots \\ x_n' = F_n(t, x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n)$$

that also satisfies the initial conditions

$$x_1(t_0) = x_1^0, \quad x_2(t_0) = x_2^0, \quad \ldots, \quad x_n(t_0) = x_n^0.$$
:::

Consider the following ODE:

$$\begin{bmatrix}
u_1' \\
u_2' \\
u_3'
\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}
0 & \overline{\kappa} & 0 \\
-\overline{\kappa} & 0 & \overline{\tau} \\
0 & -\overline{\tau} & 0
\end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix}
u_1 \\
u_2 \\
u_3
\end{bmatrix}$$

By Picard's theorem, there uniquely exists the solution $\{ u_1(s), u_2(s), u_3(s) \}$ of the above ODE satisfying $u_1(0) = D, u_2(0) = E, u_3(0) = F$. Denote

$$[a_{ij}] = \begin{bmatrix}
0 & \overline{\kappa} & 0 \\
-\overline{\kappa} & 0 & \overline{\tau} \\
0 & -\overline{\tau} & 0
\end{bmatrix}$$

1.  $\{ u_1, u_2, u_3 \}$ is orthonormal.

Let $g_{ij} = \langle u_i, u_j \rangle$. Then we have

$$\begin{align*}
g'_{ij} &= \langle u'_i, u_j \rangle + \langle u_i, u'_j \rangle \\
&= \left\langle \sum_{k=1}^3 a_{ik} u_k, u_j \right\rangle + \left\langle u_i, \sum_{k=1}^3 a_{jk} u_k \right\rangle \\
&= \sum_{k=1}^3 (a_{ik} g_{jk} + a_{jk} g_{ik})
\end{align*}$$

By Picard's theorem, there uniquely exists the solution $g_{ij}$ of the above ODE satisfying $g_{ij}(0) = \delta_{ij}$.

If $g_{ij} = \delta_{ij}$, then

$$\begin{align*}
\sum_{k=1}^3 (a_{ik} \delta_{jk} + a_{jk} \delta_{ik}) &= a_{ij} + a_{ji} \\
&= 0 \\
&= \delta'_{ij},
\end{align*}$$

which means that $\delta_{ij}$ is the unique solution. Hence, $\{ u_1, u_2, u_3 \}$ is orthonormal.

2. Let $\displaystyle \alpha(s) := \int_0^s u_1(\sigma) d \sigma + x_0$. Then $\alpha$ is $C^3$ and unit speed.

Since $\alpha'(s) = u_1(s)$ by the fundamental theorem of calculus and $u_1$ is a normal vector, $\alpha$ is unit speed.

Note that 

$$\begin{align*}
\alpha''(s) &= u_1'(s) = \overline{\kappa}(s) u_2(s) \\
\alpha'''(s) &= \overline{\kappa}'(s) u_2(s) + \overline{\kappa}(s) u_2'(s) \\
&= \overline{\kappa}'(s) u_2(s) + \overline{\kappa}(s)(-\overline{\kappa}(s)u_1(s) + \overline{\tau}(s) u_3(s)) \\
&= -\overline{\kappa}^2(s) u_1(s) + \overline{\kappa}'(s) u_2(s) + \overline{\kappa}(s)\overline{\tau}(s) u_3(s).
\end{align*}$$

Hence, $\alpha$ is $C^3$.

3. $\alpha(0) = x_0, T = u_1, N = u_2, B = u_3, \kappa = \overline{\kappa}, \tau = \overline{\tau}$.

By definition, $\alpha(0) = x_0$.

Since $T(s) = \alpha'(s) = u_1(s)$, we have $T = u_1$.

Since $\kappa(s) N(s) = T'(s) = u_1'(s) = \overline{\kappa}(s) u_2(s)$, we have $\| \kappa(s) N(s) \| = \| \overline{\kappa}(s) u_2(s) \|$, which gives that $\kappa(s) = \overline{\kappa}(s)$.

Since $\{ u_1, u_2, u_3 \}$ is orthonormal, we have $[u_1, u_2, u_3] = \pm 1$. Since $[u_1, u_2, u_3] = [D, E, F] = 1$ at $s = 0$ and $[u_1, u_2, u_3]$ is continuous, we have $[u_1, u_2, u_3] = 1$ for all $s$, which means that $\{ u_1, u_2, u_3 \}$ is a right handed orthonormal basis for $\mathbb{R}^3$.

Since $B(s) = T(s) \times N(s) = u_1(s) \times u_2(s) = u_3(s)$, we have $B = u_3$.

Since $-\tau(s) N(s) = B'(s) = u'_3(s) = -\overline{\tau}(s) u_2(s)$, we have $\tau(s) = \overline{\tau}(s)$. $\blacksquare$
